interruptionBody.generic: Ease off questions, commands, and corrections during play — the moves that quietly pull against your connection with {{childName}}.
interruptionBody.routines: Fewer commands and less repeating is what keeps bedtime, meals, and getting out the door from turning into a standoff with {{childName}}.
interruptionBody.cooperation: Fewer commands is what takes the power struggle out of each request — {{childName}} has less to push back against.
interruptionBody.selfControl: Easing off the steady stream of questions is what stops {{childName}}'s concentration from breaking every few seconds.
interruptionBody.boundaries: Trading corrections for calm acceptance is what keeps {{childName}} from going straight onto the defensive.

builderBody.generic: Spend 5 minutes a day being {{childName}}'s biggest fan — praise, describe, and reflect their play.
builderBody.routines: Narrating each small step {{childName}} takes toward the task is what builds the focus to see it through.
builderBody.cooperation: Reflecting {{childName}}'s words back is what makes them feel heard, so they dig in less.
builderBody.selfControl: A running description of {{childName}}'s play is what holds their attention and slowly stretches it.
builderBody.boundaries: Naming {{childName}}'s gentle and honest moments out loud is what makes those the moments they repeat.

calmBuilder.generic: Cutting corrections and "not like that" clears the tension out of play, so {{childName}} isn't braced for a telling-off.
calmBuilder.routines: When transitions stop coming with corrections, {{childName}} isn't already on edge before the next request.
calmBuilder.cooperation: Less criticism means fewer things for {{childName}} to argue back against, so requests stop escalating.
calmBuilder.selfControl: A steady stream of corrections keeps pulling {{childName}} out of what they're doing — dropping them protects focus.
calmBuilder.boundaries: Big behaviours often follow feeling attacked; calm acceptance lowers {{childName}}'s defences before a limit is even needed.

patienceBuilder.generic: Fewer instructions during play hand the lead back to {{childName}}, so time with you feels less like being managed.
patienceBuilder.routines: Bedtime and meals are already full of instructions — easing off in play keeps {{childName}} from tuning them all out.
patienceBuilder.cooperation: Every extra command is another chance for a standoff; fewer of them means {{childName}} pushes back less.
patienceBuilder.selfControl: Constant direction interrupts {{childName}}'s train of thought — stepping back lets them stay with a task.
patienceBuilder.boundaries: When play isn't a series of orders, {{childName}} has less to defy, and the limits that matter stand out.

presenceBuilder.generic: Swapping questions for statements takes the quiz out of play, so {{childName}} can just relax into it.
presenceBuilder.routines: A run of questions stalls a transition — describing what you see instead keeps things moving for {{childName}}.
presenceBuilder.cooperation: Questions can land like demands; fewer of them keeps the mood cooperative rather than confrontational.
presenceBuilder.selfControl: Each question makes {{childName}} stop and switch to answering — cutting them protects a fragile attention span.
presenceBuilder.boundaries: Rapid-fire questions can feel like an interrogation; easing off keeps {{childName}} from getting defensive.

confidenceBuilder.generic: Naming exactly what {{childName}} did well makes them want to do it again — you grow the behaviour you want to see.
confidenceBuilder.routines: Praising each small cooperative step through a transition makes {{childName}} more likely to repeat it next time.
confidenceBuilder.cooperation: Labeled praise for listening the first time gives {{childName}} a reason to cooperate that isn't a battle.
confidenceBuilder.selfControl: Calling out the moments {{childName}} sticks with something builds the persistence to finish tasks.
confidenceBuilder.boundaries: Praising {{childName}}'s gentle, honest, careful moments out loud makes those the behaviours that get repeated.

attentionBuilder.generic: A running description of {{childName}}'s play holds their attention on you and stretches how long they stay engaged.
attentionBuilder.routines: Narrating the steps out loud gives {{childName}} a calm, predictable script to move through the routine.
attentionBuilder.cooperation: Describing what {{childName}} is doing keeps you connected without adding demands, so cooperation comes easier.
attentionBuilder.selfControl: Describing {{childName}}'s actions as they work anchors their attention and slowly builds focus.
attentionBuilder.boundaries: Steady, calm narration keeps {{childName}} regulated and engaged, heading off the build-up to big behaviours.

communicationBuilder.generic: Repeating {{childName}}'s words back grows their language and makes them feel genuinely heard by you.
communicationBuilder.routines: Reflecting {{childName}}'s protests ("you don't want to stop yet") helps them feel understood, so the transition goes smoother.
communicationBuilder.cooperation: When {{childName}} feels heard, they dig in less — reflection defuses the talking-back before it starts.
communicationBuilder.selfControl: Echoing {{childName}}'s ideas back keeps them talking and thinking with you, extending engaged attention.
communicationBuilder.boundaries: Feeling understood lowers the frustration that often tips {{childName}} into aggression.

cooperationBuilder.generic: One clear, direct instruction at a time makes it possible for {{childName}} to actually succeed and follow through.
cooperationBuilder.routines: Clear one-step instructions give {{childName}} something doable at each point in the routine.
cooperationBuilder.cooperation: Direct, single instructions remove the wiggle room {{childName}} uses to negotiate or ignore.
cooperationBuilder.selfControl: Short, specific instructions match {{childName}}'s attention span, so they can follow without getting lost.
cooperationBuilder.boundaries: A calm, clear instruction states the boundary plainly, so {{childName}} knows what's expected before things escalate.

boundaryBuilder.generic: Following through calmly and consistently teaches {{childName}} that limits are real — without a power struggle.
boundaryBuilder.routines: When the routine holds firm every time, {{childName}} stops testing it and the daily battles fade.
boundaryBuilder.cooperation: Consistent follow-through is what makes instructions stick — {{childName}} learns that "no" means no.
boundaryBuilder.selfControl: Predictable limits give {{childName}} the outside structure to slow down and manage impulses.
boundaryBuilder.boundaries: Meeting aggression or dishonesty with the same calm, certain response every time is what makes big behaviours fade.

confidentParent.generic: With every skill in hand, you reach for the right one in the moment — connection and limits working together.
confidentParent.routines: Blending praise, narration, and calm limits lets you handle whatever a transition throws at you.
confidentParent.cooperation: Using the whole toolkit fluidly keeps everyday cooperation steady, not dependent on one trick.
confidentParent.selfControl: Moving between engagement and structure as needed gives {{childName}} consistent support for focus.
confidentParent.boundaries: Pairing warmth with firm, calm limits is what keeps the big behaviours shrinking for good.

journeyDisciplineWhy.generic: Calm, consistent limits teach {{childName}} that boundaries are real — so cooperation stops being a daily negotiation.
journeyDisciplineWhy.routines: Calm, consistent limits take the power struggle out of transitions — {{childName}} learns the routine holds firm, and the daily battles fade.
journeyDisciplineWhy.cooperation: Consistent follow-through is what makes directions stick — {{childName}} learns that limits are real, so listening stops being an endless negotiation.
journeyDisciplineWhy.selfControl: Predictable limits give {{childName}} the outside structure to slow down, stay with a task, and manage the impulse to jump to the next thing.
journeyDisciplineWhy.boundaries: {{childName}} learns that aggression, breaking things, and dishonesty always meet the same calm, certain response — and that consistency is what makes the big behaviours fade.

howToRecord.subtitle: Step-by-step guide
howToRecord.body:
Recording takes just a tap. Here's how to capture a real screen-time ending — no setup or script needed.

### 📱 Step 1: Get Ready Before the Ending
A few minutes before screen time is due to end, open Nora and go to **Screen Time Management → Today**.

* Keep your phone **within a few steps** of you and your child — on a table or shelf works well.
* You can **lock the screen** or put the phone down. Recording keeps going in the background.

### 🎙️ Step 2: Tap "Start recording"
Tap **Start recording** just before you start wrapping up screen time — before your warning, or before you say it's time to stop.

### 🏡 Step 3: Parent as You Normally Would
There's nothing to perform. Say what you'd usually say and handle it the way you usually would — **including the hard parts**. Protests, tears and negotiating are exactly what Nora needs to hear to help you.

### ⏹️ Step 4: Stop Once Things Have Settled
When your child has moved on to the next activity (or calmed down), tap **Stop recording**.

* Most endings take **10–30 minutes**.
* If you forget, Nora **stops automatically after 30 minutes**.

### 📩 Step 5: Get Your Report
Nora analyzes your recording and lets you know when your report is ready — usually within a few minutes. You'll find it on the **Today** screen under **Read report**, along with your updated plan in **My plan**.

**💡 Not able to record today?** Tap **Tell Nora** instead and answer a few quick questions. You'll still get a report and plan.

whyRecord.title: Why Record?
whyRecord.subtitle: How recording helps you
whyRecord.body:
Screen-time endings happen fast, and in the moment it's hard to notice what helped and what didn't. A short recording lets Nora see the moment the way it really happened.

### 🔍 See What Really Happens
Nora listens for the small things that make a big difference — when the warning came, the exact words used, and how your child responded. These are hard to remember accurately afterward.

### 🎯 A Plan Built for Your Family
Instead of generic tips, your report highlights **what already worked for you** and gives you **one strategy** to practice next — with steps and words that fit your child.

### 📈 Track Real Progress
Each day builds on the last. Recording helps Nora notice when a strategy is working, so you can move on — or when it's time to try something easier.

### 💜 It's Not a Test
There's no pass or fail. A messy ending is just as helpful as a smooth one — often more. Every recording is a step toward calmer transitions.

### 🔒 Your Recordings Are Private
* **Coaching Use Only:** Audio is analyzed strictly to give you insights.
* **Encrypted & Secure:** All session data is encrypted and stored securely.
* **Never Sold:** Your recordings and data are never sold to third parties.
* **Full Control:** You can delete your data or account at any time in your settings.

noraScore.title: Nora Score
noraScore.introduction: Your Nora Score is the daily balance you keep in your child's Emotional Bank Account. It measures your "Connection Capital"—the ratio of P.E.N. deposits to behavioral withdrawals made during your 5-minute Special Play Time.

excellent.summary: Your connection is overflowing! You've made massive deposits today. By maintaining high skill density and avoiding withdrawals, you have signaled to your child that they are safe, seen, and supported.
excellent.science: Your child's Upstairs Brain (logic and empathy) is fully engaged and "in the lead."
excellent.result: Your child's emotional resilience is high today. With a full bank account, they are better equipped to handle frustrations, transitions, and big feelings with ease.

good.summary: You're building a strong foundation. You have a healthy, positive balance in the bank. You are successfully practicing the "Mental Gym" workout and following your child's lead.
good.science: You are successfully balancing Cortisol vs. Oxytocin by focusing on pure connection.
good.result: Your child has a steady emotional buffer. They feel connected to you, which lowers their overall stress levels as they start their day.

payAttention.summary: Relational "leaks" happen. A lower score usually means the "Withdrawal Rate" (Commands, Questions, or Criticism) was high. This is a normal part of busy parenting, but it's a signal that the account needs a top-up.
payAttention.science: A low balance can trigger the Downstairs Brain (survival mode), making children more sensitive to stress.
payAttention.result: When "Connection Capital" is low, your child may have less emotional stamina for challenges, leading to quicker frustrations or "defense" behaviors.

praise.title: Praise (Labeled)
praise.whatItIs: Specific feedback that identifies exactly what behavior you admire. Instead of a vague "Good job," you say, "I love how carefully you are stacking those blocks."
praise.whyImportant: It builds Self-Efficacy (a child's belief in their ability to succeed). By labeling the action, you tell the child exactly which behaviors to repeat.
praise.inDailyLife: Be a "detective" for the Positive Opposite. If your child usually struggles to wait, the moment you see them sitting patiently, use a Labeled Praise: "I'm so proud of how patiently you are waiting for your snack."
praise.contextDescription: These are moments where you named exactly what your child did well — specific statements that tell them precisely which behaviour to repeat.
praise.targetNote: Your goal is {{target}} Labeled Praises per session. This is the threshold where specific feedback begins to reliably build a child's confidence and positive behaviors.

echo.title: Echo
echo.whatItIs: Repeating or rephrasing what your child says. If they say "Big tower!", you respond with "Yes, a very big tower!"
echo.whyImportant: Known as a Verbal Hug, it provides immediate validation and proves you are listening. It also acts as Language Modeling, showing correct grammar without the "withdrawal" of a correction.
echo.inDailyLife: Use Energy Matching. If your child is excited about a small discovery, match their enthusiasm with an Echo. This proves you are "in sync" with their world.
echo.contextDescription: These are moments where you repeated or rephrased your child's own words, showing you were fully listening and validating what they said.
echo.targetNote: Your goal is {{target}} Echoes this session. When your child speaks fewer than 10 times, the target adjusts to 75% of their utterances — keeping the goal realistic no matter how much they spoke.

narrate.title: Narrate
narrate.whatItIs: Describing your child's actions out loud, like a sports commentator. For example: "You're putting the red car inside the garage."
narrate.whyImportant: It creates Joint Attention, which is the most effective way to improve a child's focus and attention span. It signals that their actions are important enough for your full attention.
narrate.inDailyLife: Replace questions with narration. Instead of asking "What are you drawing?", try "You are using the green crayon to make big circles." This provides attention without putting "Performance Pressure" on the child.
narrate.contextDescription: These are moments where you described your child's actions aloud, directing your full attention to what they were doing.
narrate.targetNote: Your goal is {{target}} Narrations per session — roughly one comment per minute of play. Consistent narration sustains joint attention and supports language growth.

question.title: Questions
question.whatItIs: Even "helpful" questions like "What color is that?" or "How was your day?".
question.whyImportant: Questions are often Hidden Commands. They force the child to stop playing and "answer to you," which breaks their Flow (deep immersion).
question.inDailyLife: Use Active Silence. When your child comes home from school, avoid the "interrogation." Use P.E.N. skills to narrate their actions until they feel secure enough to share information voluntarily.
question.contextDescription: These are moments where you asked something — even well-meaning questions can act as hidden commands that interrupt your child's focus and flow.

command.title: Commands
command.whatItIs: Any instruction where you tell your child what to do (e.g., "Put the block there" or "Give me the toy").
command.whyImportant: Commands take the lead away from the child and can trigger a power struggle.
command.inDailyLife:
The 10:1 Repair Rule:

• Reduce the Volume: Aim to reduce the total number of commands you give in a day.

• The Repair: Think of every command as a $10 withdrawal. To keep the relationship "in the black," aim to use your P.E.N. skills 10 times for every 1 command you give. This repairs the connection and ensures your child is neurologically "receptive" rather than "defensive."
command.contextDescription: These are moments where you gave an instruction or directed your child's behaviour, which can shift the lead away from them.

criticism.title: Criticism
criticism.whatItIs: Any disapproval, including "No," "Stop," "Don't," or correcting a mistake.
criticism.whyImportant: It creates a Negative Attention Trap. If you give attention to a behavior by criticizing it, you may accidentally reinforce that behavior.
criticism.inDailyLife: Use Strategic Ignoring for minor misbehaviors like whining or pouting. Use a "Poker Face" and turn your attention away. The moment the behavior stops, jump back in with a Labeled Praise to reward the positive shift.
criticism.contextDescription: These are moments where you used disapproving language — saying "No," "Stop," "Don't," or correcting a mistake, which can accidentally reinforce the behaviour.

intro.p1: Many parents find it hard when screen time ends.
intro.p2: Screen-time transitions can be genuinely challenging for young children, and every child is different.
intro.p3: It’s often less about behavior and more about <hl>something deeper beneath the surface.</hl>

toysToUse.title: Toys to Use
toysToUse.subtitle: What to pick, what to skip.
toysToUse.body:
### ✅ YES: Open-Ended & Creative Toys
*Choose toys that allow your child to build, create, and imagine freely without fixed rules.*

* **Building Blocks & Construction:** LEGOs/Duplo, Mega Bloks, magnetic tiles.
![](placeholder:building-blocks)
* **Pretend Play & Figures:** Action figures, dolls, toy animals, play food, cars, or trains.
![](placeholder:pretend-play)
* **Creative Materials:** Play-Doh, coloring pages, stickers, drawing pads.
![](placeholder:creative-materials)

💡 **Why these work:** They give you plenty of opportunities to describe what your child is doing, reflect their words, and praise their creativity (**PEN** skills).

### ❌ NO: Toys to Avoid During Special Time
*Skip items that limit conversation, invite conflict, or take away control from the child.*

* **Rules or Turn-Taking:** Board games, card games, or sports (these encourage competition or adult guidance).
* **Messy or High-Frustration Activities:** Paints, glitter, intricate puzzles, or toys requiring adult assembly.
* **Screens & Electronics:** Tablets, video games, loud battery-operated toys, or watching videos.
* **Aggressive Play Toys:** Toy guns, swords, or rough-and-tumble games.

howToStart.title: How to Start
howToStart.subtitle: Clear a zone, pick toys, and press record.
howToStart.body:
### 1. Clear a Calm Zone
Find a distraction-free spot (no TV, screens, or siblings) and make it comfortable for you both (e.g., a rug or table).

### 2. Pick 2-3 Toys
Keep it simple. Pre-select just a few toys (like building blocks or creative supplies) and place them in your zone.

### 3. Scripts to Start
To begin, use this simple script:

*"Time for our Special Time! For the next 5 minutes, you decide what we play with. Pick any of these."*

### 4. Start Recording
Remember to tap **Start Recording** in the Nora app. You can lock the screen and place it somewhere nearby — it will automatically stop after 5 minutes.

howToEnd.title: How to End
howToEnd.subtitle: Wrapping up without a struggle.
howToEnd.body:
When the 5-minute timer concludes, Nora automatically ends recording and analyzing your session.

### ⏳ Step 1: Give Transition Warnings
If your child struggles with stopping, give them a head start to prepare:

* Say: **"Special Time will be over in two minutes."**
* Then: **"One minute left."**

### 📢 Step 2: Use the Ending Script
Even if you plan to keep playing, officially declaring the end releases you from the high-intensity coaching pressure.

*"Special Time is over now. I wanted to tell you that I really liked how you [insert specific praise] during our play."*

### 🎯 Step 3: Choose Your Next Steps
* **Option A: Keep Playing** — Relax and play purely for fun—no coaching or PRIDE skills required!
* **Option B: Move to Next Activity** — Clean up together, move to mealtime, or start your bedtime routine.

### Step 4: What if My Kid Does Not Want to Stop?
Kids often resist because they love your full attention, want to delay the next task (like bedtime), or feel uncertain about when Special Time will happen again.

**Quick Solutions:**

* **Use a Visual Timer:** A visual clock lets kids see the time winding down so the end isn't a surprise.
* **Pair Warnings with Next Steps:** "1 minute left! After this, you can keep playing alone or help me get dinner ready."
* **Keep a Daily Routine:** Practicing at the same time every day builds predictability.
* **Co-Regulate Meltdowns:** If tears happen, offer a hug, validate their feelings, and take deep breaths together.
* **Praise Solo Play:** Offer praise whenever you see them transition to playing independently.

siblings.title: Siblings
siblings.subtitle: Playing when you have more than one kid.
siblings.body:
**Keep Them Occupied:** Set siblings up with an engaging task (a snack, educational TV, or a special "waiting" toy) and praise them afterwards for being patient.

**Tag-Team & Switch:** If you have two parents/caregivers at home, run back-to-back sessions:

* **Round 1 (5 mins):** Parent A plays with Child 1; Parent B plays with Child 2.
* **Round 2 (5 mins):** Switch! Parent A plays with Child 2; Parent B plays with Child 1.

**Use Nap Times:** Schedule Special Time with your older child while a baby or toddler is napping for zero interruptions.

findingTime.title: Finding Time to Play
findingTime.subtitle: Fitting 5 minutes into a busy day.
findingTime.body:
Consistency matters, but flexibility keeps it doable! Here is how to fit 5 minutes into a busy day:

### 📅 Option 1: Pick a Fixed Daily Slot
Routine builds consistency. Choosing a set daily window makes Special Time an easy habit.

### 🔀 Option 2: Set 2–3 Flexible Windows
If your schedule changes, pick a few potential backup times each day.

**💡 Popular Times That Work for Parents**

* **First Thing in the Morning:** Fills your child's "emotional bank account" and sets a positive tone for the whole day.
* **Right After Work/School:** Helps you transition out of work mode and reconnects you with your child.
* **Before Bath or Bedtime Routine:** Calms your child down and makes evening transitions smoother.

countdown.name: Give simple countdown warnings
countdown.summary: Warn before time is up, so the end isn’t a surprise.
countdown.details: Use short warnings to prepare your child, such as “5 minutes left”, “2 minutes left”, “Last one, then we stop”. This helps your child adjust before the screen turns off.
countdown.why: Young children find sudden stops hard. A warning gives their brain time to shift gears before the screen goes off.
steps: Give a warning 5 minutes before the end, then again at 2 minutes.
Get close, make eye contact and say it calmly.
Name the last one: the last episode, level or song.
countdown.say: Two more minutes, then the TV goes off.

timer.name: Use a timer to make it neutral
timer.summary: Let the timer, not you, signal the end.
timer.details: A visual timer or alarm shifts the boundary from you to the routine. It supports cooperation because the timer becomes the signal, not the parent.
timer.why: When the timer signals the end, the limit comes from the routine, not from you, so there is less to argue about.
steps: Set a visual timer together before screen time starts.
Put it where your child can see it.
When it rings, point to it and follow through right away.
timer.say: The timer says screen time is done.

bridging.name: Redirect to a bridging activity
bridging.summary: Start a fun next activity yourself and invite your child in.
bridging.details: Start playing the bridging activity and describe what you’re doing to draw your child’s attention. Don’t give attention to the protest until your child joins you. Once they join, give labeled praise for their effort.
bridging.why: Going from a screen to nothing feels like a loss. A fun next activity gives your child something to move toward.
steps: Have the next activity ready before the screen goes off.
Start playing it yourself and describe what you are doing.
Ignore the protest; when your child joins, praise them for joining.
bridging.say: I’m building a tall tower with the red blocks!

consistency.title: Stay Consistent
consistency.body:
Consistency is what makes these changes work. When the limit is the same every time, {{childName}} learns that protesting doesn’t bring the screen back, and the meltdowns fade.

A heads-up: when you start holding the limit, the protests may get **louder or last longer** for a while before they get better. This is called an **extinction burst**: {{childName}} is testing whether the old way still works. It’s a sign the change is working. Stay calm, keep the limit, and it will pass.

countdown.title: Give Simple Countdown Warnings
countdown.subtitle: Give {{childName}}’s brain a clear boundary and natural stopping point before the screen turns off.
countdown.why: Sudden stops cause meltdowns. Giving a countdown with a natural stopping point (like ending after a song, video, or game round) helps {{childName}} wrap up the activity mentally, so the transition feels predictable instead of abrupt.
say: 2 minutes left before screen time ends.
This is our last song before the tablet goes away.
countdown.pause: (Then pause and wait silently: no extra questions or explanations.)

timer.title: Use a Neutral Timer
timer.subtitle: Let the timer be the boundary so you don’t have to argue.
timer.why: When you say “time’s up”, it can feel like a personal power struggle to {{childName}}. Having an objective, external cue (like a timer) makes the rule neutral and fair, taking you out of the role of the “bad guy”.
timer.sayIntro: Choose any option that fits the moment:

options.label: When Time’s Up

bridging.title: Redirect to a Bridging Activity
bridging.subtitle: Announce a fun, physical activity before screens start to make transitions effortless.
bridging.why: Stopping screens cold causes a sudden drop in dopamine. Announcing a high-value physical activity (a crunchy snack, a fun game, or a hands-on task) before screen time starts sets the expectation early. {{childName}}’s brain looks forward to what comes next instead of feeling a sudden loss when screens turn off.
